Sync mode completes multiple denoise steps within one `run_batch()`, amortizing scheduling overhead; overlap is not currently supported for sync mode. # Design ## Asynchronous run_batch() Overlap scheduling requires the scheduler to submit `run_batch()` and continue without waiting for GPU results. Some existing paths frequently synchronize the scheduler with the GPU. These paths need to return GPU tensors first and defer CPU consumption. For example, FDFO's `LowConfidence.step()` updates tokens and computes completion flags directly on GPU tensors, without calling `.tolist()` or reading GPU booleans inside the step. `DllmRunOutput.block_tokens` and `block_done` both remain tensors. ## Dependencies between batches Overlap requires the scheduler to schedule batch N+1 before receiving batch N's results. At that point, the CPU has not processed batch N's results. However, the next forward pass must use the updated block tokens from the previous step, rather than the CPU inputs that have not yet been updated. FutureMap adds `dllm_block_tokens_buf`, which stores a full block of tokens per request slot. After batch N's step, it writes the tokens into the corresponding row. Before its forward pass, N+1 reads that row and replaces its block input. This dependency stays on the GPU without passing through CPU result processing. Each row starts at `-1`, indicating that no result is available. A new block's first execution keeps the input prepared by the scheduler; FutureMap replaces it only when the row is valid. Block handoff and request completion clear the old row to `-1`, preventing the next block or a new request from reading stale tokens. `result.dllm_algo_state` retains the interface for returning algorithm state, but that state is not forwarded through FutureMap to the next step submitted ahead of result processing. Overlap for general stateful algorithms requires further adaptation. ## Request and resource lifecycle An FDFO request proceeds through block preparation, denoising, block handoff, and request completion. A request may contain multiple blocks. Both `req` and its request slot are retained across block transitions; the slot is released only when the request finishes or is aborted. ```mermaid flowchart TD S(["Request arrives"]) --> A["Prepare a new block
prepare_for_extend()"] A --> B["One denoise step

Reset to `False` after a new block is admitted. | | `req.dllm_block_id` | ID of the current block. Old and new forward passes execute in order on the same forward stream. The old block hands off resources at the start of that iteration; the next input is initialized and the ID advances only after admission succeeds. The flag does not mean that GPU execution has finished; stream ordering still enforces GPU dependencies. Until a valid completion result is processed, work submitted ahead of result processing continues denoising the current block rather than opening the next one. ## Request abort handling Aborting a request requires both invalidating old results and clearing stale data in its slot. Hi @rwang5203, this PR is now ready for review.
Could you take a look and help trigger CI? Thanks!

Thanks for the detailed design notes, they made the block lifecycle easy to follow. I compared this branch with main on one H200 using LLaDA2.0-mini, the default `--dllm-algorithm LowConfidence` launch plus `--max-running-requests 16`, 128 input and 128 output tokens, and fresh servers in alternating order. At concurrency 1 output throughput improves about 22%, GSM8K is unchanged, and cancelling live streams under overlap left the server healthy. At concurrency 16 throughput drops about 12% with overlap, about 25% with `--disable-overlap-schedule`, and about 20% with `--no-dllm-fdfo`, and the logs trace this to the phase refresh in the first comment, because that run repeats earlier prompts and hits the prefix cache. With phases refreshed before grouping, overlap beats main by about 17% at concurrency 16 and overlap off matches main, so the scheduling approach holds up well once that is fixed.

`dllm_phase` refreshes only when a block opens, so a cached-prompt request stays prefill for a whole block and decode requests wait, losing up to 25% throughput at concurrency 16. Could we refresh phases before grouping?
Overlap runs one discarded forward per completed block, a larger share of GPU work at small block sizes. Could we skip that forward for rows whose block just completed?

`step` now returns a device tensor, so the unchanged `if all(done)` in `_run_sync` converts each row to a bool, one device sync per row on every `--no-dllm-fdfo` denoise step. Consider checking `done.all()` once there.

For list results from JointThreshold or Gemma4Renoise, this adds a `done` upload and a download back on every FDFO step, although overlap stays off there. Consider dropping `device=` so list results stay on the host.

inline_comments.body: `dllm_phase` refreshes only when a block opens, so a cached-prompt request stays prefill for a whole block and decode requests wait, losing up to 25% throughput at concurrency 16. Could we refresh phases before grouping?
Overlap runs one discarded forward per completed block, a larger share of GPU work at small block sizes. Could we skip that forward for rows whose block just completed?

`step` now returns a device tensor, so the unchanged `if all(done)` in `_run_sync` converts each row to a bool, one device sync per row on every `--no-dllm-fdfo` denoise step. Consider checking `done.all()` once there.

For list results from JointThreshold or Gemma4Renoise, this adds a `done` upload and a download back on every FDFO step, although overlap stays off there. Consider dropping `device=` so list results stay on the host.

Hi @rwang5203, this PR is now ready for review.
Could you take a look and help trigger CI? Thanks!

Thanks for the detailed design notes, they made the block lifecycle easy to follow. I compared this branch with main on one H200 using LLaDA2.0-mini, the default `--dllm-algorithm LowConfidence` launch plus `--max-running-requests 16`, 128 input and 128 output tokens, and fresh servers in alternating order. At concurrency 1 output throughput improves about 22%, GSM8K is unchanged, and cancelling live streams under overlap left the server healthy. At concurrency 16 throughput drops about 12% with overlap, about 25% with `--disable-overlap-schedule`, and about 20% with `--no-dllm-fdfo`, and the logs trace this to the phase refresh in the first comment, because that run repeats earlier prompts and hits the prefix cache. With phases refreshed before grouping, overlap beats main by about 17% at concurrency 16 and overlap off matches main, so the scheduling approach holds up well once that is fixed.
